# How to pick the right free AI app when you're just getting started

> **In short:** All five major free AI apps — ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, Copilot, and Le Chat — can handle the three tasks beginners try most: writing help, answering questions, and coding assistance. They work differently under the hood, but for everyday use the real difference comes down to integrations, conversation style, and how each one fits into your existing tools.

The idea that one AI assistant is simply "the best" is a myth. Each tool is built by a different company, trained in its own way, and optimized for its own strengths. For a beginner, this actually works in your favor — it means there is a good fit for almost every need. This guide walks you through comparing the free tiers of the five most widely available assistants so you can choose with confidence, not guesswork.

## Before you start

- An internet connection and any device (phone, tablet, or computer).
- At least one free account — you do not need to pay for anything to follow this guide.
- About 15 minutes to test a few tools side by side.

## Step 1 — Decide what you actually want to do

Before looking at any app, name your goal in one sentence. The three tasks beginners try most are:

- **Writing and drafting** — emails, social posts, summaries, brainstorming ideas.
- **Answering questions and explaining things** — looking something up, learning a new topic.
- **Getting help with code** — understanding a programming concept or writing a simple script.

Most free AI apps handle all three reasonably well. The differences show up in *how well* they handle each one, and whether they fit into tools you already use.

💬 Example: "I want to draft a short email to my manager explaining why a project deadline needs to move."
You'll know it worked when you can state your goal clearly — that sentence is your comparison checklist.

## Step 2 — Compare writing and creative tools

For drafting, editing, and generating ideas, each app takes a different approach.

**ChatGPT** (OpenAI) and **Gemini** (Google) both produce quick, well-formatted drafts across many formats. They are good all-around choices for everyday writing tasks.

**Claude** (Anthropic) tends to give longer, more detailed responses and often catches nuance in longer pieces. If you write a lot of reports, emails, or documents, it may feel like a thoughtful editor rather than a speed-draft tool.

**Copilot** (Microsoft) connects directly to Microsoft Word and Outlook. If you already pay for Microsoft 365, you can generate and edit text inside those apps without switching windows.

**Le Chat** (Mistral AI) handles multilingual writing naturally — a useful advantage if you work across languages or need content in a language other than English.

All five will produce usable drafts. The question is whether one of these fits more naturally into your existing workflow.

💬 Example prompt to try in two tools: "Write a 150-word product description for a small handmade candle business."
You'll know it worked when you can compare the results side by side and spot the style differences — one may be more energetic, another more formal.

## Step 3 — Compare question-answering and knowledge tools

When you need an answer rather than a draft, the tools differ most on two points: how current the information is, and how deeply they explain.

**Gemini** draws on Google's search infrastructure for real-time information. If your question involves recent events, current prices, or anything time-sensitive, it may have an edge here on the free tier.

**ChatGPT** and **Claude** have knowledge cutoff dates — they do not browse the live web the same way. They explain concepts in depth and handle follow-up questions particularly well, making them strong for learning and research conversations.

**Copilot** uses the same underlying model as ChatGPT but displays search results alongside its answer, which some users find helpful for verifying factual claims.

**Le Chat** handles questions in multiple languages fluidly and can switch between them mid-conversation.

If your primary need is quick, up-to-date answers, try Gemini for that task. For learning and exploring a topic over several questions, ChatGPT or Claude may feel more natural.

💬 Example prompt: "Explain what a budget spreadsheet is to someone who has never made one."
You'll know it worked when the explanation uses everyday language and builds on ideas step by step — not when it throws jargon at you.

## Step 4 — Compare coding and learning tools

If you are curious about how code works or want help writing a simple script, here is how the tools line up.

**ChatGPT** and **Copilot** both generate code snippets with plain-language explanations. Copilot's advantage shows up if you write code inside Microsoft development tools — the integration is built in.

**Claude** tends to explain code in more detail and can walk through longer programs step by step, which some beginners find helpful.

**Le Chat** supports a wide range of programming languages and can switch between them in the same conversation.

**Gemini** integrates with Google tools and works well for web-related code and simpler scripts.

None of the free tiers are full development environments — they will not run your code for you. But for understanding, learning, and writing small scripts, all five are worth trying.

💬 Example prompt: "Write a simple Python script that asks for your name and prints a greeting."
You'll know it worked when you can copy the result, paste it into a free online Python editor, and run it without errors.

## Step 5 — Make your decision in three questions

After testing all five tools with the same prompt, answer three quick questions to narrow your choice:

1. Which response felt most natural to read?
2. Did any tool integrate with an app you already use (Microsoft 365, Google Workspace)?
3. Did any tool answer in the language or style you preferred?

Write the answers down. If you are a writer or content creator, you will likely lean toward ChatGPT or Gemini for their versatility. If you already use Microsoft tools every day, Copilot removes friction by living where you already work. If you value thoughtful, detailed responses, Claude may feel like the best fit. If you work across languages or want a tool that switches easily between them, Le Chat is worth a closer look.

💬 Example: After comparing results from Steps 2 through 4, note which tool you would open first if you had a real task due tomorrow.
You'll know it worked when you feel a clear pull toward one tool for one specific reason — that is a sign the fit is right, not just familiarity.

## Common mistakes

- **Assuming one tool beats all others.** Every comparison you read online reflects one person's use case. Your needs may be different. The tools are genuinely close in quality for most everyday tasks.
- **Missing tools you already have access to.** If you already pay for Microsoft 365, Copilot may already be on your computer. If you have a Google account, Gemini is a free web app. Check your existing subscriptions before signing up for something new.
- **Sticking with the first tool you try.** First impressions vary. A tool that felt awkward at first may click once you adjust how you phrase your prompts. If a tool almost worked, try rephrasing before switching.

## What this means for you

- **In everyday life:** A good AI assistant can cut the time you spend staring at a blank page, wrestling with an unfamiliar topic, or figuring out where to start on a task. The right tool makes that feel easy rather than frustrating.
- **For your business or work:** If you handle any written communication, internal documents, or basic research as part of your job, even a free AI assistant can take the first draft off your plate. The best fit is the one that connects to the tools you already use.
- **If you are just getting started:** Pick one tool and commit to using it for three real tasks this week. At the end of the week, ask yourself whether it felt natural. If yes, keep going. If not, try the next one on this list.

## Try it now

Open two of the five tools in separate tabs or windows right now. Paste the same prompt into both:

> "Give me three ideas for a weekend project I could finish in two hours with no special skills or tools."

Compare the results side by side. Notice the differences in tone, length, and creativity. That feeling of "this one speaks my language" is your signal. Trust it — and open that one first next time you have a task to tackle.
